The case study can show why the operation is abusive and how an organization can stop it. In the scenario, an operator imports an unverified list, treats delivery volume as the only success metric, and creates several superficially different templates so the messages look less repetitive. A queue retries transient errors, while a separate process keeps reintroducing addresses that were removed by a recipient. Those choices create the central failure: there is no durable suppression record, no proof of consent, and no trustworthy owner for the data. The defender can map the behavior without reproducing it. Mailbox providers see a new sender identity, rapid growth in volume, poor engagement, high complaint rates, repeated attempts to invalid addresses, and content that changes just enough to frustrate simple filters. Recipients report the messages, and the provider links the streams through authentication, infrastructure, payment, and account-recovery signals. The case study should explain that rate limiting does not make unsolicited delivery legitimate, and template rotation does not turn harassment into permission. It should also show a responsible test harness: use a closed domain or local mail sink, generate synthetic addresses, label every message as a test, and make the harness stop when a simulated recipient opts out.
